checkpoints: HMAC binds the body bytes to a secret known only to sender and receiver, so a body modified without that secret can't be re-signed to match — that's why HMAC catches tampering.
If only `body` is signed and the timestamp travels as a separate sibling header never entering the signed string, a valid `(body, sig)` pair is tied to no moment in time at all.
An attacker who captures just one real request can replay it as many times as they like and it always passes verification.
The fix is to move the timestamp inside the signed string, signing `ts.body` instead of just `body`.
This binds the signature to a specific moment, so an attacker who wants to push the timestamp into a fresh window must also recompute the HMAC, which needs the secret they don't have.
The other half of the fix lives on the receiver: a window check (e.g. ±300 seconds) comparing `age = |now - ts|` against that threshold and rejecting anything past it.
This window check is the piece that makes a captured payload expire in minutes instead of living forever.
Trade-off: a narrower window is more secure (shorter replay opportunity) but more likely to falsely reject legitimate requests when clock skew between the two machines exceeds the window.
Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is impossible.
The acknowledgement can genuinely get lost on the way back.

When that happens, you cannot simultaneously be sure you 'sent at least once' and sure you 'never sent more than once' — your only two choices are to resend (risking a duplicate) or not resend (risking a loss).
The system splits the guarantee into two halves, each owned by a different component.

The emitter guarantees at-least-once delivery: it persists the event first via a transactional outbox (same transaction as the business change) and keeps retrying until it receives an ack, since it's better to send a duplicate than lose the event.

The receiver guarantees exactly-once effect: it uses idempotency (key + body-hash + cached response) to absorb every duplicate that retries produce, so the side-effect runs exactly once even though the request may arrive more than once.
Composing the two — at-least-once on the sending side, exactly-once effect on the receiving side — yields a system that is safe end to end even when the network redelivers.
This is precisely the contract Stripe, GitHub, and every large webhook provider actually run in production, rather than an exactly-once-delivery promise that simply cannot be kept.
A module-level `const breakers = new Map()` lives only in the heap of the single Node.js process that created it, so its contents never cross a process boundary.

When a service runs as multiple horizontally-scaled worker replicas, each replica boots its own empty Map, meaning every replica ends up with an independent, disconnected view of circuit state for the same host.

Concretely, once replica B accumulates enough failures against a host and flips its local entry to `open`, replica A's own Map has no record of that — A keeps calling `allowRequest` and sending jobs to a host that is already known to be down.

A circuit breaker that only protects one process's private view of a host, rather than the host itself across the whole deployment, defeats the actual purpose of a circuit breaker in a multi-replica system.

Any deploy, crash, or scale-down destroys the process heap, so all breaker state — fail counts and `openUntil` timestamps included — is silently reset to `closed` on restart, with no signal that a previously-open circuit ever existed.

Circuit-breaker state (open/closed status, failure counts, cooldown expiry) is inherently shared, cross-replica state rather than per-worker local state, so it belongs in a store external to any single process.

The fix is to delete the in-memory Map and keep the same four pieces of state — state, fails (with a time window), a probe gate, and openUntil — as Redis keys per host (e.g. `circuit:state:<host>`, `circuit:fail:<host>`, `circuit:probe:<host>`, `circuit:openUntil:<host>`), read and written through a shared Redis client so every replica sees the same data.
A `SET circuit:probe:<host> 1 NX EX <ttl>` style key acts as a single-probe gate that stops more than one replica from sending a half-open recovery probe to the same host at the same time.

The fix is proven by running two worker instances against the same Redis, tripping the breaker via 3 failures through instance A's `recordFailure`, then calling `allowRequest` on instance B for that same host and asserting it also returns `false` — showing both instances now read one shared key instead of two independent Maps.

Plain `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` with no `SKIP LOCKED` takes row locks on the matched rows, and any other transaction whose identical query matches the same rows must wait for those locks to release rather than moving on to a different set of rows.

When two poller replicas issue the exact same `ORDER BY created_at ASC LIMIT $1 FOR UPDATE` query, the second replica ends up blocked behind the first replica's lock on the same top-N rows, so the two replicas execute serially instead of in parallel — this is why combined throughput does not improve with a second replica.

Adding `SKIP LOCKED` to the claim query (`... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`) makes a poller skip rows already locked by another transaction and claim the next available rows instead, so concurrent pollers partition the pending set into disjoint batches and genuinely run in parallel.

The `UPDATE status = 'in_flight'` must run inside the same transaction as the claiming `SELECT`, before `COMMIT`, so that a row is marked as taken the instant it is claimed — this is what stops a later poller from re-claiming the same row once locks release.

`SKIP LOCKED` is a concurrency mechanism that turns a SQL table into a scalable multi-consumer work-queue; it fixes throughput and prevents double-claiming under normal operation, but it is not by itself an exactly-once delivery guarantee.

Because `SKIP LOCKED` does not cover the crash-mid-delivery case, a row claimed and flipped to `in_flight` that never completes delivery needs a separate recovery mechanism — such as a watchdog that resets stuck `in_flight` rows after a timeout — together with the receiver's idempotency cache to guard against duplicate delivery.

Verifying the fix requires running multiple poller replicas concurrently against the same table under load and confirming that claimed-rows-per-second scales roughly linearly with the number of replicas, instead of flatlining the way it does with plain `FOR UPDATE`.

Correctness of the fix also requires confirming that no single row ID is ever claimed by two replicas at the same time, for example via an assertion or a uniqueness check across replicas' claimed batches.

Computing an HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body and running a constant-time comparison happens before the timestamp window is checked, so every incoming request pays for that crypto work regardless of whether it will ultimately be rejected.

Under a flood of stale or replayed requests, all of them are guaranteed to fail the timestamp window check, yet the receiver still performs the full HMAC computation and constant-time comparison first - burning CPU on work whose outcome was already sealed by the clock.

The window check only needs the timestamp already present in the parsed signature header and the current clock - no secret and no cryptographic work - which makes it effectively free compared to recomputing an HMAC over the body.

Moving the window check (`age > WINDOW_SECONDS`) to run immediately after parsing the header, before calling `sign()` and `constantTimeHexEqual`, lets stale requests be rejected without paying any crypto cost, while requests that survive the check still go through full signature verification.

The reorder is a pure change in cost, not in behavior: a stale timestamp was always rejected and a forged-but-in-window signature is still caught by the constant-time compare, so nothing that used to be accepted becomes rejected or vice versa.

Keeping `constantTimeHexEqual` for requests that pass the window check preserves the timing-attack resistance of the signature verification - only the order of the two checks changes, not the comparison method itself.

The fix can be verified by flooding the endpoint with out-of-window requests before and after the reorder: CPU and latency scale with the flood before the change and stay roughly flat afterward, since rejection now happens on a cheap timestamp comparison instead of a full HMAC computation.
A follow-up test with genuinely valid, in-window, correctly-signed requests must still succeed after the reorder, confirming that legitimate traffic is unaffected by the change.
Exactly three methods are exposed on the module — allowRequest, recordFailure, recordSuccess — and nothing else.
allowRequest(host) returns { allow, state, isProbe }, where state reports closed/open/half_open and isProbe signals whether this call is the one admitted probe during a cool-down.
On failure the worker calls recordFailure(host, isProbe), passing isProbe back so a failed probe re-opens the circuit immediately instead of just incrementing a counter.
recordSuccess(host) is the mirror call: on a half_open success it closes the circuit and clears state; on a closed success it's effectively a no-op.

All state — current state, a fail-count scoped to a time window, a probe key set via SET NX, and an openUntil stamp — lives in Redis keyed per host, so every worker replica shares the same view instead of a private in-memory map.
Half-open admission is enforced entirely by a SET NX gate: only the replica that wins the race gets isProbe:true and an admitted call.
Every other replica during that cool-down gets allow:false and reschedules (moveToDelayed + DelayedError) without burning an attempt.

The module stays transport-agnostic on purpose — it never imports an HTTP client or BullMQ, only answering 'may I call this host' and 'here's what happened', so it works behind any queue or caller unchanged.
A parked row carries eventId, type, targetUrl, and a forensic copy of the payload (the exact request body, not re-derived later).
A parked row carries attempts fixed at the exhausted MAX_ATTEMPTS, plus lastError and parkedAt.
A parked row carries a nullable replayedAt field that starts null.
The replay endpoint POST /api/dlq/:id/replay reads nothing from the request but the row id.

Replay writes exactly two things — replayedAt on the DLQ row (an audit stamp) and status='pending' on the original outbox_event row — without calling the receiver directly or touching circuit-breaker/retry-count state.
Replay returns a response confirming the row was requeued, e.g. { status: 'requeued' }.

Replay must be a deliberate operator-triggered action rather than an automatic retry loop, because every DLQ row already exhausted MAX_ATTEMPTS against a genuinely failing receiver, and blind auto-retry would recreate the exact flood the dead-letter split and circuit breaker exist to stop.

dead_letter gets its own table instead of a status='failed' value because the hot-path poller scan must stay small/fast, while the DLQ is operator-facing and wants its own retention, alerting, and listing endpoint.
The root bug is that the breaker's state is global/shared across the whole emitter rather than per endpoint.
One dead receiver (Merchant X) tripping that shared breaker halts webhooks to ALL merchants, not just the failing one.
The fix is keying breaker state by host:port so the isolation boundary matches reality — thousands of receivers fail independently, so each needs its own state.
With per-host keying, Merchant X tripping only blocks jobs to Merchant X, while every other merchant stays closed and keeps sending normally.
The cost of this switch is more Redis keys — one set per host instead of one shared set for the whole service.
The cost also includes an O(n) sweep over open hosts, but this stays bounded because failing hosts are always a small minority of active hosts.

Commit-then-send is unsafe: the order commits first (the database considers its job done), and if the process crashes before the send, nothing on disk recorded that a webhook was owed, so it's lost with no retry trace.

Send-then-commit doesn't avoid this, it relocates the same gap: the partner is notified before the transaction commits, so if the transaction then rolls back, the partner was told about an order that never actually existed.

The transactional-outbox fix inserts the event row into an outbox table inside the SAME transaction (same BEGIN/COMMIT) as the order insert, making the two writes atomic — either both land or neither does.
The actual HTTP call must stay OUTSIDE that transaction because a network call can hang or fail on its own schedule, and holding the DB transaction open across it would needlessly stretch locks.
A separate poller picks up pending outbox rows afterward and performs the real send with retries, independent of the original request.
The cost of this approach is one extra table plus roughly one poll-tick of latency between commit and actual delivery, in exchange for closing a previously open-ended loss window.
A fixed-delay retry policy (3 times, 2s apart) is dangerous at scale because it creates a thundering herd: everything that failed together waits the identical interval and then fires all at once.
That simultaneous pile-up is exactly what knocks the recovering receiver over again, instead of giving it room to recover.
Exponential growth spaces later retry attempts progressively further apart over time, improving the odds a retry lands right when the receiver has actually recovered.
Jitter (e.g. ±20%) desynchronizes many emitters running the identical backoff schedule so they no longer all fire at the exact same millisecond, eliminating the simultaneous spike.
The two mechanisms are independent: exponential growth decides how large the delay is per attempt, while jitter decides how spread out different emitters are at that same attempt.
Every retry attempt must re-sign with a fresh timestamp rather than reusing the original signature.
If backoff pushes a retry out far enough, a stale timestamp falls outside the signature window and gets rejected with 401 even though the secret and body are perfectly correct.
